subsystems.name: Cell source
subsystems.role: supplies the organ's own cells so the immune system accepts it.

subsystems.name: Bioink
subsystems.role: the printable 'ink': living cells suspended in a gel that holds shape and lets cells grow.

subsystems.name: Sacrificial and structural inks
subsystems.role: materials printed to create hollow channels, then removed or left as scaffold.

subsystems.name: Printer
subsystems.role: deposits thousands of droplets or filaments at cell-scale precision.
parts: extrusion, inkjet, laser or light-based print head

subsystems.name: Vascular network
subsystems.role: every cell must sit within a fraction of a millimetre of a blood supply.

subsystems.name: Maturation bioreactor
subsystems.role: perfuses the construct with oxygen and nutrients while it ripens from a blob into tissue.

buildSteps.title: Take a small biopsy
buildSteps.detail: A sample of the patient's own tissue is taken to avoid rejection.

buildSteps.title: Make stem cells
buildSteps.detail: Those cells are reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells, then coaxed into the needed cell types — heart muscle, kidney, liver or vessel lining.

buildSteps.title: Design the architecture
buildSteps.detail: Software plans the organ layer by layer, including a branching vascular tree down to capillaries.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the bioink
buildSteps.detail: Cells are mixed into a hydrogel at realistic density — tens of millions per millilitre.

buildSteps.title: Print the scaffold and vessels
buildSteps.detail: Sacrificial ink is printed first to form channels; structural and cell inks are layered around it, with the sacrificial material later washed out to leave open vessels.

buildSteps.title: Line the vessels
buildSteps.detail: Endothelial cells are seeded into the channels so the surface behaves like real blood vessels.

buildSteps.title: Mature in a bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: Perfused with warm, oxygenated medium for days to weeks, the construct fuses, stiffens and starts to function.

buildSteps.title: Test, then implant
buildSteps.detail: The organ is checked for mechanical strength, cell health and sterility, then surgically connected to the recipient's blood supply.

prerequisites.why: no technique yet keeps thick, living tissue alive — diffusion alone reaches only a few tenths of a millimetre.
billions of correctly differentiated, mature cells are needed per organ, and iPSC protocols still struggle.

prerequisites.tech: Printable hydrogels that survive and remodel
prerequisites.why: inks must be soft enough for cells but strong enough to hold an organ's shape.
organs must be kept fed and conditioned for weeks before transplant.
small patches have survived; full organs have not been demonstrated.

pathway.milestone: bioprinted skin grafts and thin tissues reaching pilot clinical use; organoids as drug-testing models
pathway.unlocks: regulatory experience and manufacturing discipline for living constructs.

pathway.milestone: vascularised tissue patches — for example heart-muscle patches and printed blood vessel grafts — tested in patients
pathway.unlocks: proof that printed tissue can connect to a living blood supply.

pathway.milestone: simple and hollow organs, such as bladder or airway structures, at clinical scale
pathway.unlocks: first whole-organ replacements built from a patient's own cells.

pathway.milestone: solid organs (kidney, liver, heart) with engineered capillary beds
pathway.unlocks: an alternative to donor waiting lists — if vascular and maturation barriers are solved.
